Chapter 6: The Power of Dissent
Imagine being the only person in a room who’s willing to say, “Wait, I see things differently.” That takes a kind of quiet courage, doesn’t it? Ruth Bader Ginsburg knew that feeling well. On the Supreme Court, she often found herself standing alone, especially as the Court’s direction began to shift. And while it might’ve been easier to just go along, Ruth leaned into something she believed deeply—the true power of dissent.
Take this one case, for example. A woman discovered she’d been paid less than her male colleagues for years. But when she finally spoke up, the Court said she’d waited too long to complain. Ruth read that decision and felt a wave of frustration. She understood how discrimination isn’t always obvious—it can hide in everyday moments, and it might take years before someone realizes what’s been happening to them. So, Ruth wrote a dissent that was clear, direct, and full of empathy. She explained, in plain language, how laws should actually help real people—not just work in theory, but in real life.
Now, her words didn’t change the ruling that day. But something fascinating happened: her message reached far beyond the courtroom. People outside the world of law started to notice. Young activists picked up her dissents and saw them as a rallying cry—proof that standing up, even when you’re outnumbered, can make a difference over time. Ruth once said, “Dissent speaks to a future age.” And she meant it. Sometimes, the seeds for real change get planted in those moments of disagreement.
What’s really striking is how Ruth approached dissent. It was never about anger or bitterness. She wrote with respect, always hoping to persuade and to show a better way forward. Over the years, some of her dissents actually inspired new laws and policies. So even when she lost a case, she was still shaping the future—one thoughtful, determined dissent at a time.
